en: If you are the hero Seytek,
Do not begin calamity and strife;
Let us remain alive.
If you call us your former enemies,
Then slaughter us all.
Our devouring enemy Sarybai—
Such was his furious savagery.
Rain down your shots upon him;
Deliver us from the bloodthirsty tyrant,
From that black fiend himself,
From the unerring eye of hell,
From the anguish of his bitter torment,
From Sarybai’s ruinous hand,
Which ravaged nations and slaughtered peoples;
Free us from him.
Release the hands of this wretched people
And earn a blessing for yourself.
Among these people fallen into your hands
There are heroes and there are khans;
Sarybai oppressed the people
And made them suffer so.
That wrathful swine became powerful,
And the treasury’s people became his slaves;
He laid low every armed man
And drove them out to die.
None escaped punishment and strife;
Not a single soul remained.
Under the venom of that infidel’s days,
We amassed great wealth
And wept until our eyes went blind.
He left no living soul in peace,
But drove and tormented everyone.
He committed deeds against the innocent
And used force upon helpless souls.
Driving us before him, Sarybai
Reduced us all to submission.
Our strength utterly failed,
Only a spoonful of blood remained in us,
Our souls nearly left us under his grip.
Gathering troops for battle,
Mustering all the people without exception,
He unleashed a terrible calamity.
Women and little children
All began to flee.
He turned every place into a road,
And driving people before him, Sarybai
Brought the whole world into bondage.
We have fallen into your hands;
If you have need of us, heroic warrior,
Let us live.
If stubborn anger seizes you,
Kill and slaughter us.
Here is the broad Kyrgyz land;
Here are the people the hero has reached.
Here is a deeply dug pit;
Here is an army, if you would destroy it all.
The champion of that army
Was exceptional in wisdom.
Those who wielded their sharp tongues
And spoke eloquently before the people,
Skilled and fluent in speech,
Whose words were sweet as sugar,
Whose sayings spoke the truth,
Quick-witted masters of discourse—
These men proved outstanding,
Strong men who judged unerringly.
Those who fired without tiring
Pressed before the ranks of heroes,
Thrusting their spears together,
Seeking out the surest path,
And kept tumbling from their horses.
Their wickedness was revealed;
Falling headlong from their horses,
Sarybai’s vast army
Submitted to brave Seytek
And now showed sound judgment.
Its champions and heroes,
Its wise and valiant men,
Those who cared for the nation,
All submitted in their ranks.
They stood firm as curdled milk, without a twitch;
The vast host lay still without stirring.
They lowered and cast down their banners,
And ceased breaking their switches;
They began their account
And abandoned everything entirely.
Like a spring flowing down the hills,
Like openly devoted friends,
They gathered around the people,
Becoming friends worth remembering,
And soon became acquainted.
Once his army had slipped from his hands,
The mighty Sarybai
Fell into such a furious rage.
His terrible wrath poured out,
And his fierce violence showed;
He stirred up a savage conflict
And slaughtered the host he encountered.
Striking with his battle-axe, he wrought havoc
And plunged the whole world into strife;
A furious battle began.
May your wretched soul run mad—
He had the people bound and cast aside.
He raged against all who dwelt there,
In a land from which no one came
And which no traveler had seen;
It proved to be a wicked nation.
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Was the khan of that wicked people.
He was the wrath of God the Creator;
He did not rule his people justly,
But did nothing except evil.
He gathered an army from that wicked nation
And destroyed the peace of peaceful folk;
Yet through all this, the wretched people
Had endured his rule.
For many years before this,
He had driven this entire nation before him,
Until Sarybai had no people left.
He disgraced and slaughtered the nation;
In fierce strife and great massacres,
How many times had he slain them?
All the multitude
Had learned the infidel’s wrath.
Unable to understand it openly,
They endured that infidel Sarybai,
The warrior who devastated nations,
Until their tears pooled like a lake.
There was no blood left to spill by the spoonful,
No hardy soul left to fight.
He would not let them sow their grain
Or reap a harvest from the land;
Driving them about and leading them astray,
He brought the people’s misery to the boil.
The people raised a mighty uproar,
Clamoring beyond all measure.
We fell into the grip of that dog with whelps;
From the hands of this infidel
We barely escaped by finding a way.
Amid slaughter we raised an outcry;
Our souls were scorched and withered.
The people murmured among themselves,
“Enough of what Sarybai has done!”
Pouring out his wrath, he turned back
And sat abandoned and bereft,
Deprived of his countless host.
His ribs felt torn apart,
His mind was utterly distracted;
Death, doom, and true disaster
Appeared above his head.
He twisted all his mustache
And tore at all his beard.
The conflict had become overwhelming;
A dreadful burden pressed upon his soul,
As, wrathful and grieving,
He lost the army he had commanded.
“I have neither tail nor mane;
I have been left a blunt beast,” he said.
“My horns have broken from my head;
I have been left hornless,” he said.
“Bereft of my beloved people,
I have become a brute,” he said.
His blood boiled and his rage swelled;
He stirred rebellion, his eyes blazing.
“What fate is coming upon me?
I am finished,” he despaired of life.
Kuyaly confronted him,
Brave Seytek grappled with him,
And Külchoro fought him.
They seized the initiative there,
But he would not submit to the three heroes.
Taking turns,
They fought him face-to-face
And waged a mighty battle.
Firing guns and loosing arrows,
They cut down all who faced them,
Waging strife beyond mortal bounds.
When a khan grows obstinate, he dies;
All who grapple in battle die.
In such a place heroes die,
And many men die together;
Great rulers die and khans die,
And all who fight die.
When the whole world gathers,
When two sides clash,
When two heroes fight,
The guiltless multitude suffers;
There is a great tumult of battle cries—
Such is the fury of holy war.
Yielding to no one who approached,
His prowess was extraordinary,
His heroism beyond compare;
He cut down all he faced,
Slaughtering as he advanced.
Yielding to no multitude,
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Grew far fiercer
Than he had been before.
The three heroes surrounded him,
And when they leveled their keen spears
And struck him from every side,
He did not so much as blink or frown;
He never bowed his head before conflict.
They could not overpower him in combat;
They roared but could not break his strength.
When they grappled, their weapons could not pierce him;
Against that wrathful, calamitous infidel,
Even blazing saxaul wood could raise no ember.
The whole world could not overcome him;
At anyone he faced, Sarybai
Kept thrusting his spear.
A savage struggle, a great calamity—
Sarybai kept creating it.
Like a wolf, Sarybai
Kept tearing apart all he encountered.
A fierce struggle, a mighty battle—
Sarybai kept waging it.
Though the three heroes surrounded him,
He did not flinch when struck with clubs,
He did not groan when cut by swords,
He did not stir when pierced by spears.
Conflict could not subdue him;
When they contended with that swine,
They could not find the slightest means against him.
Then Sarybai
Was seized by still fiercer wrath
And did not stand watching without fighting.
He was no mere nail as before;
His fury mounted and possessed him.
Brave Seytek, born of a lion,
Turned the gray kulan steed’s head;
Kuyaly’s men and Külchoro
Had taken up this cause
And now sought the way forward.
When Sarybai, son of a monster,
Unleashed his wrath,
The wide world grew narrow.
The mighty, broad-shouldered man
Grew old beneath his trials.
Under Sarybai’s venom,
Under the calamity of his wrath,
All the people despaired.
The savage lion ranged unchecked,
And all who faced him were slain.
He hunted, encircled, and cut them down;
The people endured terrible hardship.
He greatly multiplied their wounds
And showed them endless suffering.
He made his guests spend the night
And forced them to recount long tales;
He brought many forms of destruction
And shot men down from above,
Making their days one unbroken torment.
When the people spread over the summer pastures beneath the blue road,
When summertime arrived,
When snowdrop blossoms bloomed
